summary.text: Io is the innermost of Jupiter's four Galilean moons, and is slightly larger than Earth's Moon.
With over 400 active volcanoes, Io is the most geologically active object in the Solar System.
The activity comes from tidal heating: friction inside Io as it is pulled between Jupiter, Europa and Ganymede.

facts.label: Plume height
facts.value: Sulfur and sulfur dioxide plumes reach as high as 500 km

facts.label: Interior
facts.value: Silicate rock around a molten iron or iron sulfide core

facts.label: Mountains
facts.value: More than 100, and some taller than Mount Everest

items.prompt: What keeps Io's insides hot enough to drive hundreds of volcanoes?

options.label: Friction from being pulled between Jupiter and other moons
Sunlight baking its surface and heating the rock beneath
Leftover heat from a recent giant impact on its surface
Nonstop comet strikes that keep stirring its interior

items.explain: Tidal heating from friction inside Io, as Jupiter and two other Galilean moons pull on it, powers its volcanoes.

items.prompt: Most moons in the outer Solar System are mostly water ice. What is Io made of instead?

options.label: Mostly frozen water with a thin coating of sulfur
Silicate rock around a molten iron or iron sulfide core
Mostly frozen methane wrapped around a small rocky core
Mostly solid iron with no layer of rock around it at all

items.explain: Io is primarily silicate rock surrounding a molten iron or iron sulfide core, unlike most outer moons.

items.prompt: Io's surface shows yellow, red, white, black and green patches. What mainly paints it?

options.label: Frost left by Jupiter's thick, colorful atmosphere
Metal ores exposed when meteorites gouge the ground
Dust that drifts in from Jupiter's rings over time
Volcanic deposits, largely sulfur in different forms

items.explain: Plumes and lava flows from its volcanoes color the surface, largely through forms and compounds of sulfur.

items.prompt: Spacecraft in 1979 found almost no impact craters on Io. What does that point to?

options.label: A young surface, in a world that is volcanically active
A very old surface that has been worn smooth by wind
A protective shield of thick gas that stops impacts
A location in space that no stray rocks ever visit

items.explain: Voyager found a young surface with no obvious impact craters on a world full of volcanic features.

items.prompt: On 7 January 1610 Galileo saw Io and Europa as a single point of light; the next night he saw two. What explains the first night?

options.label: Clouds over Padua hid one of the two moons
The two moons were passing in front of each other
His 20x telescope was too weak to split them apart
Europa was too faint to show before the next night

items.explain: The low power of his telescope could not separate the two, so they were recorded as one point of light.

items.prompt: Several of Io's volcanoes throw plumes far above the surface. What do those plumes mainly consist of?

options.label: Water vapor from an ocean hidden under the crust
Sulfur and sulfur dioxide thrown up by eruptions
Ash and carbon dioxide, as on Earth's volcanoes
Methane gas leaking out of frozen surface lakes

items.explain: Several volcanoes produce plumes of sulfur and sulfur dioxide as high as 500 km above the surface.
